role: Legal secretary at a law firm
headline: A legal secretary at a firm of thirty-odd people in Urumqi, tracking filing and appeal deadlines, binding case files and scheduling hearings. When the winter roads close, one court summons means working out how to cover three hundred kilometers
unit: A law firm of more than thirty people in Urumqi
level: You know the document formats by heart and you type fast. What a fixed period is, or which document dies if it's a day late, you have not yet handled yourself
intro: The firm is on the seventeenth floor of an office building near South Lake. Work starts at ten o'clock Beijing time, and in winter there's only just a little light outside the windows at that hour. Your desk is next to the printer, and on it is an old pad from a three-hole punch. Sister Cheng, who is training you, gives you your first task: bind this year's closed case files. Every page in here, she says, weighs more than you or me.
salary_note: Estimate: legal secretarial jobs in Urumqi pay slightly less than in inland provincial capitals. There's a year-end bonus based on the team's billings.

facts.label: Where AI is moving in
facts.value: Drafting publicity copy and case summaries

facts.label: Open positions
facts.value: 12 related listings nationwide, 0 in this city (the job database is mostly campus hiring and internships)

day: You open the case ledger. Deadlines due today are in red, those within three days in orange. Sister Cheng got in twenty minutes before you and has already gone over the red row.
You run to the court's filing window, holding number 47. Your copies are prepared per the number of defendants plus two. The person ahead of you gets turned away, and you quietly count yours again.
Lunch downstairs, two hours later here than in the rest of the country. Lawyer He dictates a letter while he eats, and you type it into your phone without dropping a word.
You phone the clerk at the Changji court to confirm a hearing time. She says the scheduling system has changed, and you rewrite this summons's time in three different places.

Punch, thread, back cover, page numbers: a case file comes together in the order of its index. The thread has to be pulled tight and the knot tied at the back. Sister Cheng turns two pages and has you take it apart.

A client comes to the front desk for the third time to ask about progress, and settles on the sofa. You bring him water and tell him the lawyer is in court today, and that what you can do is write down his question.
On your way home the sky hasn't quite gone dark. You hunch your shoulders and walk to the bus stop, the packed snow slick and loud underfoot.

ladder.title: Trainee Legal Secretary
ladder.focus: Send and receive documents, bind files, run filings, learn the firm's procedures and confidentiality rules

ladder.title: Legal Secretary
ladder.focus: Manage the team's case ledger and deadlines, schedule hearings and travel, liaise with court clerks

ladder.title: Senior Legal Secretary
ladder.focus: Own the team's procedures and document quality, train new hires, help with billing and settlements

ladder.title: Law Firm Office Manager
ladder.focus: Manage the firm's conflict checks, seals, archives and inspections, and mediate among partners

ladder.title: Law Firm Operations Director
ladder.focus: Run the firm's financial processes, information systems and staffing; sit in on partner meetings

ai_tasks.name: Coordinating between courts and clients
ai_tasks.how: Whether a clerk will check a schedule for you, and why a client has called for the third time today, take a person to deal with.

ai_tasks.name: Keeping confidentiality and judgment
ai_tasks.how: What can be said to a client, and which documents can't go into which system, a person has to answer for.

ai_tasks.name: Drafting publicity copy and case summaries
ai_tasks.how: AI can handle drafts and rewrites. A person checks the legal language and makes sure nothing confidential gets out.

ai_tasks.name: Case ledgers and deadline reminders
ai_tasks.how: AI can calculate deadlines, send reminders and check filing. Which deadline really matters takes a person to judge and coordinate.

ai_tasks.name: Proofreading document formats
ai_tasks.how: AI can bring a document up to standard. Each party's name and each amount must still be checked by a person.

ai_tasks.name: Preparing meetings and events
ai_tasks.how: AI can draft agendas and notices. Venues, guests and the sense of proportion are a person's work.

events.e_binding: In the first file you bind, the page numbers jump from 90 to 92. Sister Cheng has you check the whole thing, and it turns out you took a double-sided page as single. That day you learn a term: missing page.
events.e_conflict: Before taking a new case you run a conflict check, and find that a shareholder of the opposing company is the legal representative of a former client of the firm from three years ago. The partner goes quiet when you tell him. The firm doesn't take the case. The person who came goes to a different firm the same day.
events.e_snow: The winter wind zone closes the road. Lawyer He has a hearing in Karamay, the expressway is shut and the flights have been canceled. You wrote the application to postpone two days ago, and you attach a screenshot of the closure notice. The clerk says on the phone that she has it.
events.e_ems: The date on the return receipt for a mailed document is illegible, and the lawyer urgently needs to know when the other side got it. You spend half an hour at the post office counter, then go to the delivery station, where a courier helps you dig the original slip out of his basket.
events.e_may: Every May comes the annual review of the firm and its lawyers. The justice bureau needs materials in several copies, and each lawyer's practice file must be checked. You and the office staff cover the conference room floor, and in three days every form has been reconciled.
events.e_year_end: Year's end is settlement season: fees to collect, invoices to issue, closed cases to archive. In the last week of December you never leave before nine. It's twenty below outside, and the office radiators are hot enough to give you a headache.
events.e_wrist: Your right wrist begins to hurt from punching and pulling thread, plus the daily keyboard. The physiotherapist asks if you play badminton. Sort of, you say. Case files.
events.e_cervical: Your eyes go farsighted earlier than your friends', and the small print in case files has to be held farther away. Your neck follows. You raise your monitor on two copies of the Civil Code, which is what these two books have mainly been used for lately.
events.e_clerk: For three years you've been on the phone with a certain court clerk without ever meeting her. One day in a hallway you recognize her by her voice, and both of you laugh. She says your firm's materials are the most complete. That sentence seems to you worth more than a bonus.
events.e_e_filing: Online filing and electronic service come in everywhere, and the lines at the filing window shrink by half. You no longer have to run errands, but every system update changes the upload format, and every time some scanned copy gets bounced.
events.e_ai_doc: The firm starts using AI for first drafts, and a statement of representation appears in minutes. A young lawyer sends one to you to proofread, and you find a cited article number that doesn't exist. When Lawyer He hears about it, he has a notice sent around the entire firm.
events.e_ai_post: The firm's social media post, which used to take you half a day, now takes AI ten minutes. A partner says this frees you up for other things. You ask him what. First, he says, read what it wrote.
events.e_client_wait: One client comes in once a week, always with a bag of fruit that he puts down before leaving, just to ask about progress. The matter goes on for nearly two years. The day it closes he brings the lawyer a silk banner and you two boxes of Korla pears.
events.e_flight: You go with a partner to a hearing in Hami, and the flight is delayed past midnight. You hold the document case on your knees in the departure hall and go over tomorrow's evidence index again. This case never goes in the hold.
events.e_young: A new trainee lawyer who has passed the bar is twelve years younger than you, calls you sister and asks you to stick on his receipts. Three years on he is a lawyer in his own right, still calls you sister, and you're still sticking on his receipts.
events.e_winter_kid: Work ends by Beijing time, and so does your child's school. On winter nights you get home at eight-thirty, and your child is doing homework in full darkness. You ask what he learned today. You asked me that yesterday, he says.
events.e_archive: The firm moves, and more than twenty years of archives have to go into a new storeroom. You count them box by box by year, list those whose retention periods are up, write the destruction list and ask a partner to sign. Once it's signed, someone says this firm is older than they'd thought.
events.e_director_retire: The founding director retires, and the new one wants to change how money is divided. A partners' meeting runs past midnight, and you refill the tea outside the door four times, while the voices inside rise and fall.

c_deadline.title: Two days left to appeal
c_deadline.situation: Only two days are left in the appeal period. Lawyer He is out of town, and the appeal petition has only just come back signed. It's snowing hard, the post office won't promise anything, and the online system is under maintenance today. Filing it in person at the Changji court would take half a day round trip, on bad roads.

options.label: Drive it there yourself
options.result: It takes twice as long as usual to reach Changji. You file it ten minutes before the window closes and get the receipt. Your hands are a little unsteady the whole way back.

options.label: Wait for the system and mail it too
options.result: You go both ways at once: send it by EMS and wait out the system, uploading at eleven that night. When Lawyer He gets back he says it's fine, but next time don't let it get to that day.

c_client_ask.title: Can we win?
c_client_ask.situation: A client grabs you while the lawyer is out. You're here every day, he says, you must know. Can we win this or not? You've been following the matter, and you do have some idea. His eyes are red.

options.label: Say he should ask the lawyer
options.result: You say that isn't for you to say and that you'll help him book the lawyer's time. He sighs. You bring him a cup of water, and the awkwardness passes.

options.label: Reassure him it should be fine
options.result: He's grateful, and later tells the lawyer that your secretary said it'd be no problem. Lawyer He calls you into his office, and closes the door.

c_senior.title: Applying for Senior Legal Secretary
c_senior.situation: Sister Cheng is moving to administration, and the Senior Legal Secretary post on the team is open. It means managing the workflow of five or six lawyers and training new people. Lawyer He says give it a try, but you'll have to pick up every call before ten at night.

options.label: Give it a try
options.result: You take over Sister Cheng's ledger and split one Excel sheet into three. For the first three months you know better than the lawyers where they'll be next month.

options.label: You'd rather not manage people
options.result: You say you only want to serve your lawyers well. Someone new becomes senior, you go on leaving on time, and this winter feels a bit warmer than the last.

c_exam.title: The bar exam
c_exam.situation: The younger people at the firm are all taking the national bar exam. You have only an associate degree and would need to get a bachelor's through self-study first, four or five years in all. If you pass you become a paralegal, and then a lawyer. Those four or five years of evenings and weekends will be gone.

options.label: Self-study and the bar
options.result: You study after work until midnight, and come to know the Civil Procedure Law better than Lawyer He does. The first attempt misses by a few points. Next year you take it again.

options.label: Skip it, this job's fine
options.result: You tell yourself that a legal secretary is a profession too, which you sometimes believe and sometimes don't. But your evenings remain your own.

c_ai.title: Setting up the team's AI workflow
c_ai.situation: AI use has become chaotic, and someone has put client materials into a public tool. A partner asks you to make the rules: which materials can be used, how to write prompt templates, who proofreads the output. There's no budget for this, but nobody at the firm knows the procedures better.

options.label: Take this on
options.result: You write twelve pages of rules. Number one is “Who must approve materials leaving the firm.” The lawyers find it tiresome, and within six months are all using your templates.

options.label: Not a secretary's job
options.result: You pass. The IT department issues a regulation, very long, that no one reads, and everybody goes on doing things their own way.

c_split.title: The team is breaking away
c_split.situation: Lawyer He is taking his team out to start his own firm, and asks you privately if you'll go. Twenty percent more pay, an office in the Xinshi District, and everything built from scratch. If you stay, the director says, the admin side will eventually be yours.

options.label: Go with Lawyer He
options.result: You move into an office with no curtains, and in the first week even have to borrow a stapler. The pay is higher, and the work has doubled.

options.label: Stay at the old firm
options.result: The day Lawyer He leaves, he puts your coffee cup back on your desk. You stay, and begin learning to manage the partners you used to just deliver documents to.

c_admin.title: Applying for Law Firm Office Manager
c_admin.situation: The Law Firm Office Manager post is changing hands. The job covers seals, archives and conflict checks, plus whatever the partners don't want to deal with. You're not a lawyer, and at meetings some people will act as if you're not there.

options.label: Apply
options.result: You take custody of the firm's seal and turn the seal-use log into a triplicate form. In your first month a partner loses his temper at you because his stamp came a day late.

options.label: Stay with the team
options.result: You stay on the team, and the lawyers trust you. An outside hire takes the position, and in her first week she comes to ask you where the firm's seal is kept.

c_court.title: Contract court clerk
c_court.situation: The court is hiring contract clerks. The pay is a little lower than yours. The work is trial transcription, steady, without clients coming in to ask about progress. You've become a very fast typist, and your friend the clerk tells you to try.

options.label: Apply
options.end: You change badges and sit down in a corner of the courtroom, your hands on the stenotype keyboard. Now you are the one who answers the phone to confirm times.
options.result: You spend three days going over your ledger with the new person.

options.label: Don't go
options.result: You say you'll think about it, the firm needs you just now. In the afternoon the printer jams again.

c_merge.title: Merging into a national firm
c_merge.situation: The firm is merging into the regional office of a large national firm. Headquarters has its own systems and procedures, and administrative jobs are being trimmed. You can take a payout and go, or accept a place at the shared service center, entirely online, with task orders from a different time zone.

options.label: Take the payout
options.end: On the day headquarters' system goes live, your account expires. You export your final ledger to a spreadsheet and leave a one-page note saying after what hours you should call certain lawyers.
options.result: You sign the agreement. It takes half an hour to clear out your desk.

options.label: Move to the shared center
options.result: You work from home at two monitors, taking orders from branch offices across the country. At ten in the morning colleagues in the east are already on their second reminder.

endings.retire: The month your retirement goes through, the system shuts off your account, and the reds and oranges of the ledger go on glowing on someone else's screen. The case files you've bound over the years fill a whole storeroom, every knot tied at the back. When the retention periods end someone will destroy them, and even then it will show whether the thread was pulled tight.
endings.burnout: Your wrist reaches the point where you can't lift the punch, and your eyes can't manage small print. You go through your deadlines one by one with whoever is taking over, stay an extra week, and make sure there's no red row within the next three months. It's snowing the day you leave. People at the firm tell you to come visit.

stages: Your day is sending and receiving, copying, binding, standing in line at the court's window to file, and preparing each document in the required number of copies. The punch, the cotton thread and the page-numbering stamp are your three tools, and each week Sister Cheng spot-checks them; one wrong page and the whole volume comes apart. The lawyers' names, and their tempers, you have a month to memorize.

You manage the case ledger for several lawyers: filing, evidence, hearings, appeals, each point in the table, a reminder three days out and another one day out. You confirm hearing times with clerks, book travel and pack document cases, and pick up clients' calls, saying what can be said and leaving out what can't.

One team's procedures and document quality are yours. You go over new people's letters, follow lawyers' invoices and fees, and lead the year-end archiving of closed cases. When a lawyer makes a mistake, you try to arrange things so he finds it himself. The difference from the level below: you no longer wait for instructions; you tell the lawyers what they need to do next week.

You manage the firm's seals, archives and conflict checks, and also the justice bureau's annual review. Whatever the partners can't conveniently say to one another's faces often comes to you to carry, and you have to think about whether to carry it, and how much. The seal-use log in your hands is more sensitive than any contract.

You attend partner meetings without a vote, and answer when anybody asks about procedures and numbers. Financial workflows, the case-management system, hiring and the firm's move all pass through you. You negotiate contracts with the software company, and you talk to the youngest lawyer about why he can't skip this step.
work: The filing window rejects a submission that's one copy short. You run to the print shop at the court gate, at half a yuan a page. Standing ahead of you is another firm's secretary, who nods.

Sister Cheng has you sort a box of documents in reverse chronological order. When you've finished she pulls out the thirteenth sheet and says this is a return receipt, and it goes with the letter it belongs to.
You print the judgment Lawyer He asked for three times. The first time, the final page is missing; the second time, the page numbers are wrong; the third time, he puts it in his bag without looking.
An evidence deadline in the ledger lands in the middle of the National Day holiday. You count it to the first working day after, phone the clerk to make sure, and mark it orange.
The summons says Courtroom 3, but when you get there it's been changed to 7. You've arrived half an hour early and see the change on the notice board, and text the lawyer on his way.
A lawyer's case has to go to Karamay. You label everything in order of hearing. The first bag has copies of ID and the power of attorney, the second has original evidence.
A new secretary has mixed up one page between two clients' files. You catch it before it goes out, have her check it again, and add a line to the checklist: read the heading on every page.

At year's end, the title on one of Lawyer He's fee invoices is wrong, and the client's accountant sends it back. You issue a red-letter correction and a new invoice, and while you're at it make a table of every client title for the team.
A young lawyer's letter runs three pages. You stick on a note: could the first paragraph be the last paragraph? The next day he deletes the last two pages.
In the conflict system, a new client's name closely resembles an old client's subsidiary. You pull the registration forms and ask two partners to sit down at the same table.
One month in the seal-use log is entirely in one assistant's handwriting. You look into it and find a partner had her collect the seal for him. You add a rule on proxy collection.

The case-management software company doubles its quote. You print out three years of support tickets and ask about them one by one, which were their own bugs, and in the end you knock off forty percent.
At a partner meeting you show each team's collection cycle as a chart. You don't write any names, and everyone can tell. Starting that quarter, payment reminders go out a good deal more often.
past: You go to junior high in Changji, and your parents work at a cement plant. On winter mornings you ride behind your father on his motorcycle, your ears full of wind.

Your father's work unit owes him back pay and he hires a lawyer to write it up, while you wait at the door of the law firm. A young woman in a sweater is typing at flying speed, and it strikes you as a respectable kind of work.
You study legal secretarial work. You're first in typing class and second in legal document formats. The one who came first ends up selling apartments.
Interning at a court you help the clerks, binding case files until your fingers blister, and you see parties to a case wait all day on the corridor bench.
You apply for jobs after graduation. The interview at the firm is a typing test, five minutes, no more than three typos to pass. Sister Cheng reads what you've typed and asks when you can start.

late.pension_note: Estimate: over thirty years of contributions at Urumqi's base bring a pension of about 45 percent of final monthly pay. Bonuses don't count.
scenes: The first winter you don't have to get anywhere. On snowy mornings you watch people walking and judge which shoes will slip. Most of your judgments are correct.

The compound is renewing its contract with the property manager, and someone from the owners' committee brings it over to show you. First you count the pages. One stamp across the seam is missing, and you pencil a little circle in the corner.

You go to stay with relatives in the east for a while. They eat dinner at six in the evening and you aren't remotely hungry. Two o'clock is lunchtime here, and your stomach has run on Urumqi time for thirty years.

Nowadays filing doesn't take a trip to the window, and nobody punches and threads anymore. The print shop at the court gate has closed and become a store selling phone cases. Who knows what half a yuan buys now.
You wear a wrist brace, can't type, and learn to use voice input. The first sentence comes out with three wrong words. You go to fix them, and then remember you don't have to.

The neighborhood mediation office needs someone to help write up agreements, half a day a week. You write slowly with your left hand, and when you've written out the parties' names you check them against the ID once more.
Your eyes aren't good and you have to enlarge the text. Even enlarged you can't get through the contract terms on your phone. You learn to tap “Agree,” and each time it rankles a bit.
In the first year your calendar is still full of red and orange. In spring you turn off all the reminders, and find that your phone has gone remarkably quiet.

A former colleague comes for tea and says AI now calculates deadlines more accurately than anyone, and that the only time it slipped up was on the Spring Festival make-up workdays. The two of you laugh for quite a while. You're both willing to tell this a few more times.
You receive an agreement for picking up a delivery, with dozens of boxes to tick. You read each one to the end, while the courier grows somewhat anxious outside the door.
With any letter that comes, you still check the date at the end before the contents. You read a friend's invitation the same way, and she asks you if something's wrong with you.
Recipes, prescriptions, utility bills: everything in your home is filed in reverse chronological order. When family members want to find something, first they have to learn the system.

closing.retire: Ten o'clock, and it has only just got light out. There's no red row in your day. You put water on and wait for it to boil.
closing.burnout: Snow lands on the windowsill and melts a little. You take off the brace and lay it on the table, and slowly turn your wrist around once.
closing.end: You pass a cotton thread through the needle's eye and sew up an old padded jacket of your child's, tying the knot at the back, pulled tight.
